Project Title: Low-noise Pre-amplifier Design
Description: This project will investigate designing, building and thoroughly testing low-noise pre-amplifiers for microphones (and other sensors).

Project Title: Auto Focus
Description: An automatic focusing system will be developed for a Blackmagic Micro Cinema Camera. Part of this project involves developing an interface between the camera and a computer. What the camera is looking at should be displayed on the computer screen, and if a user clicks on a particular part of the image, the software should focus the camera there.

Project Title: Electronically Assisted Astronomy
Description: Electronically assisted astronomy (EAA) is becoming popular. Instead of looking directly through the eyepiece of a telescope, you can instead look at a real-time image on a computer screen generated by processing the output of a video camera connected to the telescope. This project will explore various image processing algorithms for enhancing the image displayed on the screen. For this project, the processing can be done either on a computer or on an FPGA board.

Project Title: Single pixel camera
Description:
What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Conventional digital cameras, e.g. in smartphones and tablets, are based on silicon image sensors with millions of pixels. It is possible however to make a camera using just one pixel. These are called “single pixel cameras” and use spatial light modulators like those found in computer projectors. These spatial light modulators are placed before or after the object to be imaged. They apply time-varying patterns, and synchronized intensity measurements are made with the single pixel. An algorithm takes these measurements and generates an image. This approach allows images to be collected at wavelengths outside the capabilities of image sensor technologies. Potential applications include the visualization of hazardous gas leaks using infrared single pixels.

In this project, single pixel cameras will be investigated. A prototype single pixel camera has been built at the University of Melbourne, but considerable scope for improvement exists (e.g. in resolution, imaging modality and frame rate). These improvements will be the topic of this project.

Why is this issue important?
Silicon based image sensors are highly effective as digital cameras for consumers. These work well for visible wavelength light, but cannot record images at infrared (IR) wavelengths. Cameras that record images at infrared wavelengths are highly effective for applications that include night vision, the direct visualization of hazardous gases, thermal imaging and visibility through fog and smog. IR cameras based on image sensors exist but are expensive. Single pixel cameras operating in the IR offer the possibility of being much cheaper.

What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?
The project makes use of electrical and electronic engineering concepts that include electronic systems (e.g. the combination of hardware and software in the single pixel camera), signal processing (e.g. the generation of the image from the measured data), and computer programming (e.g. the system is controlled by Python scripts). A standard background in electrical and electronic engineering is needed. Specialized skills and knowledge are not needed.

What do you envisage as an expected outcome of the research?
As discussed, a basic prototype has already been constructed at the University of Melbourne. Considerable scope for improvement exists. This includes, but is not limited to, increasing the image acquisition speed, improved the imaging resolution, and expanding the imaging modality beyond that of grayscale imaging. These improvements, and other innovations to be made by the project group, are the expected outcome of the research.

Project Title: Numerical study of solar chimney
Description: The fluid flow over a bluff body (such as a circular cylinder and a flat plate) is one of the most studied areas in fluid mechanics research. In many investigations, the bluff body  is considered in isolation and the neighbouring walls or other objects are often assumed to be too far away to have any consequences on the flow field near the cylinder. However, in many engineering applications, such as in heat exchangers and the flow past dividers in chemical processing plants, characteristics of the flow field  are affected by the presence of nearby walls.  In this project, you will use latest state of the art computational fluid dynamics tools to study the fundamental physics of the fluid flow field over a bluff body in a confined environment.

Project Title: Bubble Motion in Ocean Waves
Description: This project will deliver data on the behaviour of air bubbles under ocean waves. Coordinated experiments and computer simulations will measure and simulate where bubbles go and how they block underwater noise. The construction of offshore wind turbines, proposed to begin in Australia as soon as 2025, generates dangerous noise levels as piles are hammered into the seabed, potentially damaging marine-mammal hearing. In Europe's North Sea, clouds of bubbles from air hoses on the seabed form 'curtains' blocking this noise, protecting small, dolphin-like animals which are not endangered species. However, unlike in Europe, Australia's wind-turbine sites feature ocean swell and turbulence that would degrade existing bubble curtains. Furthermore, Australian wind-turbine farm sites are frequented by huge, endangered whales, the Southern Right Whale and Blue Whale, and also the Humpback Whale, bringing us over a quarter of a billion dollars annually in tourist income. Expected project outcomes would be an understanding of bubble behaviour in ocean swell, valuable for models of how bubble clouds drive the ocean's absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide; and a prediction of the sound-blocking ability of bubble clouds in ocean swell. This would enable new bubble-curtain designs for a number of ocean industries, and may also give Australia's defence industries an edge in new technologies for the control of low-frequency underwater noise, a key to detecting submarines over very long distances.

Project Title: Computational study of ember dispersion and fluid flow in Wildland Urban Interface during bushfires
Description:
Bushfires pose a significant threat to communities located in the Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) areas where bushland meets human settlements. While firebreaks such as roads and cleared vegetation are designed to slow the spread of fire front, they cannot prevent ember showers. These embers - tiny burning particles - can travel hundreds of meters on the wind, crossing firebreaks and igniting homes and structures. Current operational models predict the movement of the main fire front but do not account for ember-driven ignition, which is often the primary cause of property loss. This project aims to bridge that gap by developing and enhancing computational models to predict ember dispersion and assess ignition risk in WUI areas.
You will:
•	Work on a fast, real-time dispersion modelling code optimized for GPUs and CPUs.
•	Incorporate additional physics and realistic scenarios to simulate ember transport and deposition.
•	Collaborate with experts from the School of Agriculture, Food and Ecosystem Sciences (fire behaviour) and the Department of Mechanical Engineering (fluid dynamics and computational modelling).
This is an exciting opportunity to apply computational fluid dynamics, high-performance computing, and environmental modelling to a real-world problem with significant societal impact. Your work will be a first step toward predicting ember-driven fire risk and improving community resilience against bushfires.

Project Title: AI-enabled cost governance for complex infrastructure and megaprojects (Industry access)
Description:
Cost management and control in complex infrastructure and megaprojects remains vulnerable to forecast error, weak early-warning signals, fragmented data, and limited transparency, especially across long lifecycles and multi-actor governance environments. This project investigates how AI methods (predictive analytics, machine learning, and NLP) can be used to improve cost accuracy, explainability, and early risk detection, and what ethical governance arrangements are required to adopt AI responsibly in cost decision processes.
Megaproject cost overruns and late risk detection have large public value consequences, shaping affordability, service performance, and trust in infrastructure delivery. AI tools are increasingly available, but without a governance lens they can introduce bias, opaque decision-making, data quality failures, and accountability gaps—particularly when models influence budgets, contingencies, claims, and change control. A focused, applied study can produce a practical AI-enabled governance and cost-control framework that strengthens decision quality while meeting expectations for fairness, accountability, and data integrity.
Key skills / knowledge needed to investigate the issue
Project governance and cost management in infrastructure/megaproject settings (controls, contingencies, change, reporting)
AI/analytics literacy (predictive modelling concepts; ML model types; evaluation metrics; limitations)
Natural language processing concepts (unstructured text sources such as progress reports, RFIs, claims, meeting minutes)
Data governance and ethics (fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, data integrity, auditability)
Digital project controls / 5D-BIM awareness (cost integration with scope/schedule, information flows)
Research methods (structured literature review, expert interviews or case-based document analysis, framework synthesis)
Expected outcome of the research
A practice-oriented AI-based framework for cost governance in megaprojects, including:
an AI use-case map across the cost lifecycle (estimation → budgeting → change/claims → forecasting → benefits realisation interfaces),
a set of design principles for integrating AI into project controls and governance (roles, decision rights, assurance, escalation),
an ethical governance model for responsible AI adoption (fairness tests, accountability and human-in-the-loop controls, data integrity requirements, audit trails), and
an implementation checklist / maturity rubric aligned with 5D-BIM and project control processes to guide adoption and evaluation.

Project Title: Enhancing safety training through LLM Assisted questioning and feedback for OHS management
Description:
The construction and infrastructure sector continues to face persistent challenges in occupational health and safety (OHS) training, particularly in preparing workers to recognise hazards and make appropriate decisions in complex and dynamic site environments.

This project builds on an existing VR based construction site training environment and focuses on enhancing the training experience through large language model (LLM) assisted questioning and feedback. Rather than further developing the VR environment itself, the project concentrates on embedding an intelligent question and feedback layer that can interact with trainees in natural language, prompt critical reflection on safety decisions, and provide context sensitive guidance during and after training activities.

The project will design and integrate LLM assisted functions to support interactive questioning, scenario based prompts and tailored feedback aligned with occupational health and safety procedures and site rules. The design of the training interactions will be informed by surveys, interviews and focus groups with safety practitioners, trainers and students, and will be refined through iterative user testing.

The expected outcome is an enhanced VR based OHS training system with an intelligent and adaptive question and feedback capability, demonstrating how LLM assisted tools can improve learning quality, engagement and transfer of safety knowledge to real construction and infrastructure practice.

Project Title: Benchmarking skylight material selection for optimised lifecycle cost and risk
Description:
This capstone project develops an evidence based benchmark to support insurance premium setting and risk classification for buildings with skylight systems. The project compares common skylight materials, including acrylic, polycarbonate and glass, in terms of their lifecycle cost, damage susceptibility and long term financial risk.

The study will examine how material choice influences the likelihood and consequences of typical loss events, such as impact damage, weather related failure and ageing related degradation, as well as the associated inspection, maintenance and replacement requirements. 

A lifecycle cost and loss modelling framework will be developed for each skylight material option, combining initial installation cost, planned maintenance, inspection regimes and scenario based damage events. The results will be used to establish comparative risk and cost benchmarks that can inform insurance underwriting assumptions, risk loading and premium differentiation between different skylight material configurations.

The outcome of the project is a practical and transparent benchmarking tool that supports insurers and building owners in setting insurance conditions, determining inspection requirements and improving the alignment between skylight design choices and long term insurance and asset management outcomes.

Project Title: Physics-Informed Neural Modelling of 2D Unsteady Flow Over a Circular Cylinder Using Sparse CFD Data
Description:
This project explores physics-informed neural network (PINN) modelling for unsteady flow past a two-dimensional (2D) circular cylinder by combining computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with modern machine learning (ML) techniques. Flow past a cylinder is a classical benchmark in fluid mechanics, and unsteady Reynolds-averaged Navier—Stokes (URANS) simulations are widely used in practice to capture vortex shedding and force fluctuations. At the same time, PINNs offer a promising way to incorporate governing equations directly into data-driven models, potentially enabling accurate flow reconstruction using limited observations. However, for unsteady flows in practical regimes, it remains unclear how much data is required for such models to reliably recover key flow features.

The aim of this project is to quantitatively investigate the data efficiency of physics-informed neural models using sparse data obtained from numerical simulations. The neural model will explicitly enforce incompressible flow physics while being guided by a limited number of simulation-derived observations, such as probe-like velocity measurements. The central question is how the accuracy of predicted flow fields and engineering quantities depends on the amount and placement of available data when the governing equations are enforced.

The project will be carried out in two stages. First, students will develop and validate the complete workflow using a lower Reynolds number laminar unsteady case (e.g. Re = 100), allowing the modelling approach to be tested in a controlled and computationally inexpensive setting. The validated framework will then be applied to a practical unsteady flow regime using two-dimensional URANS simulations at Re = 3900, which forms the main focus of the study.

Using the URANS solution as a baseline, students will conduct a systematic numerical study to assess how sparse simulation-based observations influence the recovery of key unsteady flow characteristics. Performance will be evaluated using engineering-relevant quantities such as mean drag coefficient, time-varying lift coefficient, and vortex shedding frequency. The emphasis is on understanding the practical capabilities and limitations of physics-informed learning with limited data, rather than developing new turbulence models or neural network architectures.

The expected outcome is a reproducible computational workflow and a quantitative analysis of sparse-data requirements for physics-informed modelling of unsteady flows. The project is designed to be suitable for a team of three to four students over two semesters and has potential for dissemination as a conference paper or technical report.

Project Title: X-band motion sensor design
Description: X-band motion sensors exploit the Doppler effect to facilitate the detection of moving objects. A combination of low power and efficient design enables their safe application in a range of settings, including healthcare, security, and autonomous vehicles. In this project, a cheap, commercially available, safe, low power X-band microwave motion sensor will be reverse engineered to understand and model its operation. Trade-offs and improvements in its specifications will be explored, including bandwidth, beam width, sensitivity, and range. Intended project outcomes include a detailed analysis of the existing sensor, and at least one revised design implemented in simulation and hardware.

Project Title: Scalable optimal control via learned symplectic transformations
Description: General non-quadratic optimal control problems are notoriously difficult to solve in practice, due to a curse-of-dimensionality afflicting the Hamilton-Jacobi equation involved. However, for some special classes of such problems, a solution characterization known as a Hopf-Lax formula allows efficient computations to proceed in remarkably high dimensions. Moreover, it is known that broader classes of such problems can be explored via the use of symplectic transformations applied to the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics. In this project, solvability of certain non-quadratic optimal control problems will be investigated via learning, wherein an unknown symplectic transformation relating each problem to a known Hopf-Lax formula is approximated and learned via a specialized neural network architecture.

Project Title: Seal Integrity Control for Single-Serve Pet Food Trays (Mars Petcare)
Description:
About Mars Petcare: Mars Petcare is a global leader in pet nutrition and health, with a strong manufacturing footprint in Australia. The Wodonga site produces a range of single-serve wet pet food products that are distributed nationally and internationally. Mars is committed to delivering high-quality, safe, and reliable products to consumers, while continuously improving operational efficiency and reducing waste across its manufacturing network.

Scope of the Project:
This project focuses on seal integrity issues in single-serve pet food trays at the Mars Petcare Wodonga site. Marks on seals are the primary cause of quality holds and sorting activities, leading to increased waste, cost, and risk of open seals reaching the market. The project will review current testing methods, control limits, inspection practices, and product disposition processes, and propose data-driven short- and long-term solutions to improve seal performance, reduce product waste, and lower sorting costs.

Project deliverables may include:
1.	Analysis of current seal testing methods, defect trends, hold volumes, and associated waste and sorting costs.
2.	Data analysis and modelling of seal defect occurrence and process capability under current control and action limits.
3.	Development and feasibility assessment (technical and economical) of recommended short- and long-term process improvements.
4.	Final project report and presentation to key stakeholders

Project Title: Automatic Road Asset Identification
Description:
a) Key issue / problem to be investigated
City and highway authorities maintain thousands of “road assets” — signage, guardrails, lane markings, lighting poles, manholes, drainage structures, etc. — but the current inventory and inspection process is largely manual. Crews drive the network, record observations on paper or tablets, then enter data into asset‐management software. This approach is slow, expensive, hazardous for field staff, and prone to omissions. The research problem is to design and evaluate an automatic, vision-based system that detects, classifies, and geolocates road assets from imagery collected by a standard vehicle-mounted camera (dash-cam or smartphone) plus low-cost GNSS/IMU sensors.

b) Why this issue is important
Safety & cost: Automated identification reduces the time inspectors spend on the roadway and cuts data-collection budgets.

Data quality & frequency: Authorities gain near-real-time, high-resolution inventories, enabling predictive maintenance and faster response to damage after storms or accidents.

Scalability: A low-cost, camera-first workflow can cover rural roads and developing regions that cannot afford LiDAR vans or frequent manual surveys.

Policy & sustainability: Accurate asset data underpin carbon-aware maintenance planning (e.g., prioritizing resurfacing vs. replacement) and help agencies comply with “state-of-good-repair” reporting mandates.

c) Key skills / knowledge needed

Computer Vision & Deep Learning

d) Envisaged expected outcome
A Prototype that can capture road assets with confidence scores
A conference paper summarising model architecture, performance, and cost–benefit analysis.

Project Title: 360-Degree Camera-Based Hazard Detection and Safety Inspection System for Indoor Spaces
Description:
This capstone project investigates how 360-degree cameras can be used to inspect indoor and outdoor spaces and automatically detect potential hazards. The project will explore the use of panoramic imagery, computer vision, VLMs, and AI-based object detection to support safer and more efficient inspection of buildings, rooms, corridors, laboratories, construction areas, and other indoor environments.

a) Key issue or problem to be investigated
Manual safety inspections can be time-consuming, inconsistent, and dependent on the experience of the inspector. Some hazards may be missed, especially in complex or crowded spaces. This project investigates whether 360-degree cameras can provide a more complete visual record of a space and help detect visible hazards such as blocked exits, exposed cables, trip hazards, unsafe storage, cluttered walkways, fire risks, damaged surfaces, and other potential safety issues.

b) Why this issue is important
Identifying hazards early is important for reducing accidents, improving workplace safety, supporting compliance, and maintaining safe indoor environments. A 360-degree camera can capture the full surrounding space in a single image or video, which may improve inspection coverage compared with standard photos. Combining 360-degree imagery with AI could help organisations perform faster, more consistent, and better documented safety inspections.

c) Key skills or knowledge needed
The project will require knowledge of 360-degree image capture, image processing, computer vision, object detection, and machine learning or deep learning. Students will also need skills in data collection, image annotation, and Python programming. Experience with tools such as OpenCV, YOLO, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or similar platforms would be useful.

d) Expected outcome of the research
The expected outcome is a working prototype that can process 360-degree images or videos of indoor spaces and identify selected safety hazards. The project should produce a clear workflow for capturing images, detecting hazards, and presenting results through annotated images, a basic dashboard, or an inspection report. The final output should also discuss the accuracy, limitations, and future potential of using 360-degree cameras for automated safety inspection.

Project Title: Development of geopolymer materials using combined activators for high-temperature performance
Description: This project aims to develop advanced geopolymer materials using combinations of chemical activators to achieve superior performance at elevated temperatures. Geopolymers are promising alternatives to ordinary Portland cement due to their lower carbon footprint and excellent thermal resistance. Capstone students will assist in designing and preparing geopolymer mixes using industrial by-products activated by different chemical systems. They will carry out mortar casting, specimen preparation, and curing under controlled conditions. Specimens will then be cyclically exposed to high temperatures (up to 600°C) and evaluated for residual mechanical properties, mass loss, thermal conductivity, and microstructural changes. Carbon emissions and material costs will also be calculated and compared across mix designs. Through this work, students will gain valuable hands-on experience in materials design and testing, contributing to the development of a sustainable and cost-effective binding system.

Project Title: Internal aerodynamics of racing tires (Alpine F1 Team)
Description:
The industry partner for this project is BWT Alpine F1 team.

The tire temperature in F1 racing is a major performance factor. Too hot, and the tire wears out too quickly, but too cold, and the tire loses its grip. The optimum temperature lies in a narrow window. A few degrees Celsius off optimal conditions can cost tenths of seconds in lap time.

In general, the air in the tire is highly unsteady. Under typical conditions, the motion is turbulent, characterised by chaotic swirls, modulated by acceleration and braking cycles. This turbulence can enhance the aerodynamic heat transfer between the rim and tire by 10—100 times relative to that of stationary air that rotates as a rigid body. The purpose of this project is to improve our understanding towards reliable and accurate predictions of this heat transfer. In general, this heat transfer depends on the temperature difference between the rim and the tire, the tire's angular velocity and the tire's linear acceleration. This heat transfer dictates the tire temperature, and in this way informs race strategy.

This is the third time we are running this project. In 2023, we formulated the problem and identified the parameter space relevant to racing conditions. In 2024, we explored the range of heat-transfer behaviours. We found that the heat transfer in the tire is strongly suppressed by rotation, and therefore severely overestimated in standard CFD (with consequences on tyre temperature and race strategy), a finding now submitted to a research journal. For this third time, we will tackle remaining open questions, such as whether some of the idealisations are justified and what opportunities are available for flow control. The precise scope will be developed in consultation with Alpine F1 Team, and depend strongly on team technical preparation and ability, motivation, professionalism, etc.

This project requires professionalism, dedication, time management and motivation. Research activities of this project include, but are not limited to, 1) performing direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations, 2) mathematical and physical analysis of racing-specific conditions, 3) flow visualisations/animations and analysis/interpretation of simulation data, 4) development of presentation skills and of technical communication through written reports

Project Title: Aerodynamic drag reduction by metamaterial surfaces
Description:
This is a research project, the goal is to potentially convert the project to a PhD.

Metamaterials, loosely speaking, are materials that do not exist naturally. They are engineered to have "weird" behaviours/properties (e.g. negative Poisson's ratio). This research project will explore the potential of metamaterials to beneficially interact with a turbulent flow towards reducing drag.

Aerodynamic skin friction drag comprises 50% of passenger aircraft drag. Airlines and aircraft fleet operators are sensitive to even 1% drag change, as fuel costs needed to overcome drag dominate all other costs. Today, only one strategy exists for reducing drag (a surface texture called riblets), and so drag reduction is the holy grail. All aircraft manufacturers know that the most efficient aircraft will rule the skies. The issue is pertinent for Australia, which relies heavily on air travel to connects its people and for defence.

Outcome: an exploratory analysis that can help to identify metamaterial designs worth further investigation.

We will also emphasise and develop presentation and report-writing skills.

Project Title: Modelling hydrogen–methane flames for fuel‑flexible gas turbines
Description: Adding hydrogen to natural gas is a promising pathway for decarbonisation, but realising its potential requires that combustion-based energy systems become more fuel-flexible. Gas turbines are a key technology in this transition, so enabling them to operate reliably on hydrogen–natural gas blends requires a detailed understanding of the combustion behaviour for these mixtures. This project will focus on modelling a premixed flame fuelled with these blends. The team will work in close collaboration with Prof Talei's group to implement the flame configuration in a solver commonly used for gas turbine simulations, validate the numerical results against the experimental data of an experimental setup at the University of British Colombia (UBC). The aim of this project is to deliver insights into flame behaviour, with the ultimate goal of informing gas turbine designs and safe operational envelopes for hydrogen-enriched fuels.

Project Title: AI-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting and Asset Extraction from Video Data
Description:
This capstone project investigates how videos can be used to create realistic 3D scenes using 3D Gaussian Splatting and how AI can be applied to extract useful assets from the generated 3D environment. The project focuses on converting ordinary video footage into an interactive 3D representation and then identifying, segmenting, and extracting objects or features such as buildings, furniture, infrastructure elements, equipment, signs, vegetation, or other visible assets.

a) Key issue or problem to be investigated
Traditional 3D modelling can be slow, expensive, and labour-intensive. Creating accurate 3D models often requires specialised equipment, manual modelling, or complex photogrammetry workflows. This project investigates whether video-based 3D Gaussian Splatting can provide a faster and more accessible method for creating realistic 3D scenes. It also explores how AI can be used to automatically detect and extract meaningful assets from these scenes.

b) Why this issue is important
Fast and low-cost 3D scene reconstruction is important for digital twins, asset management, facility inspection, construction monitoring, urban modelling, heritage documentation, and infrastructure management. Many organisations already collect video data, but this data is often not fully used for 3D analysis. By turning videos into 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes and extracting assets using AI, the project can support better spatial understanding, faster documentation, and more efficient decision-making.

c) Key skills or knowledge needed
The project will require knowledge of 3D reconstruction, computer vision, image and video processing, AI-based object detection or segmentation, and basic 3D data handling. Students should also understand camera movement, video frame extraction, scene capture quality, and how visual data can be converted into a 3D representation. Experience with Python, Gaussian Splatting tools, YOLO, Segment Anything Model, PyTorch, or similar tools would be useful.

d) Expected outcome of the research
The expected outcome is a working workflow that takes video footage as input, generates a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene, and applies AI methods to detect, segment, or extract selected assets. The final output may include an interactive 3D scene, annotated assets, extracted object masks, asset labels, and a simple report or interface showing the detected assets. The project should also assess the accuracy, quality, limitations, and practical use of this method for real-world asset extraction.

Project Title: Project Title Cooperative Drone Communication and Real-Time Video Streaming System
Description:
a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used for surveillance, inspection, search and rescue, and intelligent transportation applications. A key challenge is enabling multiple drones to communicate and cooperate while transmitting data to a ground station in real time. This project investigates the design and implementation of a simple multi-drone communication system in which two small drones exchange basic telemetry information (e.g., position, speed, and status) while simultaneously capturing and streaming live video to a laptop-based ground server.

b) Why is this issue important?
Multi-agent drone systems are becoming increasingly important in engineering applications because they can cover larger areas, provide redundancy, and improve operational efficiency compared to a single drone. Understanding drone-to-drone communication and real-time video transmission provides students with practical experience in wireless communications, networking, embedded systems, robotics, and intelligent transportation technologies. The project also introduces concepts relevant to future connected autonomous systems and smart-city applications.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?
Students will require or develop knowledge in:

Basic electronics and embedded systems.
Wireless communication technologies (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, ESP-NOW, or similar).
Computer networking and communication protocols.
Python or similar programming languages.


d) What do you envisage as an expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a functional prototype consisting of:

Two small drones equipped with communication modules capable of exchanging basic telemetry data such as position and status information.
A ground-based laptop server that receives and displays telemetry data from both drones.
Real-time video streaming from one or both drones to the laptop server.
A demonstration of coordinated drone operation and communication.
A final report documenting system design, implementation, performance evaluation, communication reliability, video latency, and recommendations for future improvements.

Project Title: Design and Development of a Solar-Powered Multi-Sensor UAV with Real-Time Ground Station Communication
Description:
a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are widely used in environmental monitoring, surveillance, disaster response, and infrastructure inspection. However, their operational time is often limited by battery capacity, and their sensing capabilities are usually constrained by payload and power limitations. This project investigates the design and development of a solar-powered drone equipped with multiple lightweight sensor systems (temperature, audio, video, infrared, laser, and LiDAR) and the ability to transmit real-time data to a laptop-based ground station. The system will also incorporate a custom-designed 3D-printed drone frame to optimize weight, aerodynamics, and payload integration.

b) Why is this issue important?
Extending UAV flight time using renewable energy sources such as solar power is critical for long-duration missions in environmental monitoring, agriculture, smart cities, and disaster management. Integrating multiple sensing modalities into a single aerial platform enhances situational awareness and data quality. Furthermore, real-time transmission of multi-sensor data enables faster decision-making and improves the effectiveness of autonomous systems. This project provides students with hands-on experience in sustainable engineering, embedded systems, sensor fusion, additive manufacturing (3D printing), and wireless communication—skills that are essential for next-generation aerospace and smart infrastructure systems.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?
Students will develop and apply skills in:

UAV design, assembly, and flight control systems.
Solar energy harvesting and power management circuits.
Embedded systems and microcontroller programming (e.g., Arduino, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi).
Integration of multiple sensors including temperature, audio, infrared, laser, and LiDAR modules.
Wireless communication and real-time data streaming to a ground station (Wi-Fi, RF modules, or LTE-based systems).
3D CAD design and additive manufacturing for drone frame development.


d) What do you envisage as the expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a fully functional prototype UAV system that includes:

A lightweight, 3D-printed drone frame designed for optimized payload and solar panel integration.
A solar-powered energy system capable of extending flight endurance beyond conventional battery-only operation.
Integration of multiple sensors (temperature, audio, infrared, laser, and LiDAR) mounted on the drone.
A real-time communication system transmitting sensor data to a laptop-based ground station.
A demonstration of stable flight with simultaneous multi-sensor data acquisition and live streaming.
A technical report detailing system architecture, energy efficiency, communication performance, sensor accuracy, and design trade-offs.

Project Title: Performance Monitoring of Permeable Pavement Systems in consideration of land use, application, technology and design (Merri-bek City Council)
Description:
Permeable Pavement Systems are emerging across Australia and globally as Water Sensitive Urban Design Solution, especially in dense urban environments where space, traffic load and surface run-off intensity make some other solutions less appealing. Permeable pavements can reduce surface run-off volume, delay the peak flow, improve quality of infiltered water and if design allows, improve ground water recharge and have a positive impact on urban canopy. 

Despite the long legacy of using permeable pavements in different applications and in a variety of ground conditions, there is limited research on their long-term performance, across different designs, land use and over different ground conditions. Majority of existing data is limited to certain technologies and over a small area and in certain applications. This knowledge gap is one of the barriers in uptake of permeable pavements in urban settings.

This research project aims to look at performance of permeable pavements in terms of infiltration capacity, surface temperature, surface movement and surface stress across different applications (e.g. footpath, shared path, tree protection zone, driveways and so), and for variety of designs and over different ground conditions. Field testing combined with analytical work will provide a basis to develop (perhaps) the first ever comprehensive picture on performance of these systems in Australia.
The selected team will be supervised by academic experts in Pavement Geotechnics (Faculty of Engineering) and Urban Water Management (Faculty of Science) and Industry (local government).

Project Title: Preventing firedamp’ explosions in mines by predicting and managing gas discharge from coal seams
Description:
Context. On May 22, 2026, a catastrophic explosion occurred at the Liushenyu Coal Mine in Qinyuan County, Shanxi Province, China, resulting in at least 82 confirmed deaths and over 120 injuries. This incident is considered the deadliest mining disaster in China in over a decade and was caused by a "firedamp" explosion. This mining term describes the ignition of a dangerous mixture of flammable gases entering the mine shafts from coal seams that continuously release methane gas following dewatering (drainage) for extraction. If ventilation systems are inadequate, this gas can accumulate to explosive concentrations and a A single spark from equipment, electrical faults, or friction can ignite the mixture.
Investigations indicate that the Liushenyu mine had been previously cited for severe safety hazards due to the high gas content of the coal. The disaster is largely being attributed to a failure to follow established safety protocols, such as immediate evacuation upon detecting dangerous gas levels. Yet, there is plenty of historical evidence that gas discharge from fractured coal can occur locally and in bursts that cannot be managed easily. Since the beginning of the 20th century, firedamp explosions have cost the lives of thousands of miners and the Liushenyu disaster demonstrates that a better quantitative understanding can safe lifes. 

Technical background. Ventilation is currently the primary defense against firedamp explosions; however, its effectiveness depends on synchronizing ventilation intensity with the dewatering of fractured coal seams. A critical challenge is that even minor drainage can flip fracture conditions from water-saturated to gas-dominated, increasing gas mobility by orders of magnitude. As gas desorbs and expands into fractures, it displaces remaining water, creating a positive feedback loop. This mechanism often triggers the rapid gas discharges that lead to spontaneous combustion, mine fires, and catastrophic explosions.
Despite these high risks, predicting gas discharge triggered by drainage—whether deliberate or involuntary—is not standard industry practice. While some operators utilize dual-continua (fracture-matrix) models, these fail to account for how gas discharge rates fluctuate with the changing fracture-matrix interface area. A fit-for-purpose model must quantify these drainage risks to inform operational management strategies and provide real-time, actionable data to prevent ignition and explosions.

Objectives. This project aims to develop and apply a high-fidelity Discrete Fracture and Matrix (DFM) simulator to generate the training datasets required for a surrogate machine learning (ML) model. This ML surrogate will be used to accurately predict gas discharge rates from coal seams under realistic operational conditions. The DFM simulator will be implemented within the Open-CSMP++ framework - or a comparable high-performance platform - with fracture geometries and mine-shafts modelled using Rhinoceros™ or similar CAD tools.

The project will be executed through the following primary tasks:
1. Develop a conceptual model of the component processes relevant for desorption and gas flow in fractured coal seams. 
2. Implement this DFM simulator using CSMP’s hybrid FEM-FVM simulation framework or other.
3. Build and parameterise a series of input models for simulations at different scales.
4. Calibrate the DFM model calibration with experimental data from the literature.
5. Develop and train a ML/AI based surrogate model / cyber-physical system (CPS) assimilating real-time data from mining operations and providing management recommendations for dewatering and ventilation. 
6. Run test cases and analyse them to understand mining scenarios leading to firedamp explosions.

Project Outcomes and Impact. This project offers a high-impact research opportunity to develop next-generation solutions for mine safety. Students will contribute to the following key outcomes:
•	Advanced Physical Insights: Gain a deep, mechanistic understanding of gas and water flow in rock fractures and how fracture geometry, saturation levels, and drainage-induced pressure changes dictate gas discharge in complex coal seams.
•	Next-Generation Simulation: Help build a specialized DFM-to-ML simulation framework—a powerful new tool capable of real-time forecasting gas discharge dynamics that traditional models overlook.
•	Safety Engineering Standards: Define new, data-driven guidelines for underground degassing strategies, directly addressing the critical need for proactive accident prevention.

Career and Industry Impact .This research is more than an academic exercise; it is a pathway to real-world industrial impact. The technologies developed will be primed for trial application, with significant potential for patenting, licensing, and commercialization through the University of Melbourne’s innovation pathways.
By participating, you will tackle a genuine engineering challenge with high stakes, working at the intersection of computational physics and machine learning. This is an ideal foundation for students looking to make a measurable difference in worker safety while gaining specialized skills highly sought after by the mining and resource sectors.
A comprehensive documentation package, including foundational literature and technical references, will be provided to all interested team members.

Project Title: Design and Development of a Solar-Powered Multi-Sensor UAV with Real-Time Ground Station Communication
Description:
a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are widely used in environmental monitoring, surveillance, disaster response, and infrastructure inspection. However, their operational time is often limited by battery capacity, and their sensing capabilities are usually constrained by payload and power limitations. This project investigates the design and development of a solar-powered drone equipped with multiple lightweight sensor systems (temperature, audio, video, infrared, laser, and LiDAR) and the ability to transmit real-time data to a laptop-based ground station. The system will also incorporate a custom-designed 3D-printed drone frame to optimize weight, aerodynamics, and payload integration.

b) Why is this issue important?
Extending UAV flight time using renewable energy sources such as solar power is critical for long-duration missions in environmental monitoring, agriculture, smart cities, and disaster management. Integrating multiple sensing modalities into a single aerial platform enhances situational awareness and data quality. Furthermore, real-time transmission of multi-sensor data enables faster decision-making and improves the effectiveness of autonomous systems. This project provides students with hands-on experience in sustainable engineering, embedded systems, sensor fusion, additive manufacturing (3D printing), and wireless communication—skills that are essential for next-generation aerospace and smart infrastructure systems.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?
Students will develop and apply skills in:

UAV design, assembly, and flight control systems.
Solar energy harvesting and power management circuits.
Embedded systems and microcontroller programming (e.g., Arduino, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi).
Integration of multiple sensors including temperature, audio, infrared, laser, and LiDAR modules.
Wireless communication and real-time data streaming to a ground station (Wi-Fi, RF modules, or LTE-based systems).
3D CAD design and additive manufacturing for drone frame development.


d) What do you envisage as the expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a fully functional prototype UAV system that includes:

A lightweight, 3D-printed drone frame designed for optimized payload and solar panel integration.
A solar-powered energy system capable of extending flight endurance beyond conventional battery-only operation.
Integration of multiple sensors (temperature, audio, infrared, laser, and LiDAR) mounted on the drone.
A real-time communication system transmitting sensor data to a laptop-based ground station.
A demonstration of stable flight with simultaneous multi-sensor data acquisition and live streaming.
A technical report detailing system architecture, energy efficiency, communication performance, sensor accuracy, and design trade-offs.

Project Title: Project Title Cooperative Drone Communication and Real-Time Video Streaming System
Description:
a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used for surveillance, inspection, search and rescue, and intelligent transportation applications. A key challenge is enabling multiple drones to communicate and cooperate while transmitting data to a ground station in real time. This project investigates the design and implementation of a simple multi-drone communication system in which two small drones exchange basic telemetry information (e.g., position, speed, and status) while simultaneously capturing and streaming live video to a laptop-based ground server.

b) Why is this issue important?
Multi-agent drone systems are becoming increasingly important in engineering applications because they can cover larger areas, provide redundancy, and improve operational efficiency compared to a single drone. Understanding drone-to-drone communication and real-time video transmission provides students with practical experience in wireless communications, networking, embedded systems, robotics, and intelligent transportation technologies. The project also introduces concepts relevant to future connected autonomous systems and smart-city applications.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?
Students will require or develop knowledge in:

Basic electronics and embedded systems.
Wireless communication technologies (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, ESP-NOW, or similar).
Computer networking and communication protocols.
Python or similar programming languages.


d) What do you envisage as an expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a functional prototype consisting of:

Two small drones equipped with communication modules capable of exchanging basic telemetry data such as position and status information.
A ground-based laptop server that receives and displays telemetry data from both drones.
Real-time video streaming from one or both drones to the laptop server.
A demonstration of coordinated drone operation and communication.
A final report documenting system design, implementation, performance evaluation, communication reliability, video latency, and recommendations for future improvements.

Project Title: Propagation pathways of Southern Ocean swell and their modulation along the southeast Australian coast
Description:
Swell is a type of ocean wave that is generated by winds far away and then travels long distances across the ocean, even after the wind that created it has weakened or disappeared. Although the Southern Ocean is widely recognised as a major swell source for the Southern Hemisphere, the pathways, timing and partition-specific characteristics of Southern Ocean swell reaching mid-latitude Australian waters remain less well quantified. In particular, it remains unclear how remotely generated Southern Ocean swell can be distinguished from locally generated wind-sea, how long it takes to propagate toward southern Australia, and how its arrival patterns vary seasonally and regionally. These uncertainties are important because Southern Ocean swell can substantially influence wave exposure along the southern Australian coast, even under weak local wind conditions. In addition, large-scale climate modes, such as the Southern Annular Mode and El Niño–Southern Oscillation, may affect both swell generation in the Southern Ocean and its subsequent propagation into the Australian region.
This study addresses this gap by tracing Southern Ocean swell propagation toward southern Australia using long-term reanalysis wave partitions and by assessing its modulation by large-scale climate modes and regional coastal geometry.

Project Title: Water Sustainability at Standley Chasm
Description:
a) What is the key issue to be investigated?

The project will investigate the long-term sustainability of water resources at Standley Chasm. This includes understanding current and future water demands associated with tourism operations and local residents, assessing the reliability and resilience of water supplies, evaluating water quality requirements for different uses, and identifying opportunities to improve water management practices.

b) Why is this issue important?

Standley Chasm is a significant cultural landscape managed by the Western Arrernte Traditional Owners and is a major tourism destination in Central Australia. Reliable access to water is essential for supporting tourism operations, local community needs, and the Traditional Owners' responsibilities to care for Country. With increasing visitor numbers and potential future pressures from climate variability, there is a need to better understand the sustainability of existing water resources and identify appropriate management strategies for the future.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge that will be needed to investigate the issue?

Students may draw upon skills and knowledge from environmental engineering, water resources engineering, sustainability assessment, hydrology, water quality analysis, systems thinking, data analysis, and stakeholder engagement. The project will also require students to work collaboratively with the Traditional Owners and other stakeholders to understand local priorities and incorporate cultural, environmental, and operational considerations into their analysis.

d) What do you envisage as an expected outcome of the research?

The project is expected to provide an evidence-based assessment of water demand, water quality requirements, and the robustness of existing water supplies at Standley Chasm. Outcomes may include recommendations for improving water sustainability, identifying opportunities for more efficient water use, and developing options to support long-term water management that aligns with Traditional Owner aspirations, operational requirements, and care for Country.

Project Title: Developing a Conversational Digital Portal for Intelligent Querying of Cadastral Survey Data
Description: Digital cadastral systems contain important legal and spatial information about parcels, boundaries, easements, restrictions, survey marks, connections, annotations, and related survey records. However, this information is often difficult to access and interpret, particularly for users who are not familiar with cadastral terminology, survey plans, and complex data structures. The key problem investigated in this research is how conversational artificial intelligence can be used to support more intuitive access to digital cadastral information by allowing users to ask complex questions in natural language. Improving access to cadastral information can support surveyors, land administration professionals, planners, government agencies, and non-specialist users. A conversational cadastral portal could reduce the time required to search and interpret land information, improve transparency, and make digital cadastral data more accessible to a wider range of users. The expected outcome of the research is a prototype conversational digital cadastral portal that enables users to ask natural-language questions about cadastral survey and land information and receive structured, accurate, and understandable responses. The project is expected to demonstrate how conversational AI can improve access to complex cadastral datasets and support the modernisation of land administration systems.

Project Title: Integrating Operational Reliability and Maintenance-Aware Modelling into MILPBased Trading Optimisation for Large-Scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (AGL)
Description:
Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are increasingly deployed for energy arbitrage
and ancillary service markets; however, existing optimisation frameworks are
predominantly driven by economic objectives and rely on simplified representations of
system behaviour. These models typically assume fixed efficiencies and neglect the
impact of degradation, operating conditions, and maintenance constraints, leading to
discrepancies between optimised schedules and real-world execution. Prior research
has shown that such simplifications can result in state-of-charge (SOC) drift, unfulfilled
energy delivery, and increased balancing costs, highlighting the need for more accurate
operational modelling. [Operationa...EEE Xplore]
At the same time, recent reliability-focused studies demonstrate that BESS
performance is strongly dependent on battery lifetime degradation, operating
conditions (e.g., temperature, depth of discharge, SOC), and cell-level heterogeneity.
These factors significantly influence system reliability and can lead to accelerated
degradation or weak-link effects that reduce overall available capacity and operational
effectiveness.
This project proposes the development of a maintenance- and operation-aware
modelling framework that integrates degradation and reliability considerations into an
existing Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP)-based trading optimisation engine.
Leveraging AGL Energy’s extensive historical operational, asset, and trading datasets
from large-scale BESS assets, the study aims to bridge the gap between economic
optimisation and physical asset behaviour.
The proposed approach introduces three key enhancements to the existing
optimisation framework:
1. Degradation-aware modelling, incorporating condition-dependent battery
degradation functions that account for cycling behaviour, SOC profiles, and
thermal conditions;
2. Operational reliability constraints, representing system-level capacity
availability as a function of battery state-of-health (SOH) and linking degradation
to probabilistic delivery performance;
3. Maintenance-informed decision variables, including degradation cost proxies,
availability constraints, and reliability importance indices to prioritise
operational regimes that balance revenue generation with asset longevity. 
The methodology combines data-driven parameter estimation from field
measurements with simplified, tractable model formulations suitable for integration
into linear optimisation. The framework will be evaluated using historical trading
scenarios, comparing baseline optimisation results against maintenance-aware
formulations in terms of revenue, reliability, degradation impact, and schedule
feasibility. 

The expected outcome is a scalable and production-ready optimisation
enhancement that enables BESS trading strategies to explicitly account for operational
risk and maintenance requirements. By aligning dispatch decisions with long-term
asset health and reliability objectives, this work aims to improve real-world execution
accuracy, reduce lifecycle costs, and support more sustainable and resilient operation
of grid-scale battery assets.

Project Title: "Virtual Sensor" for Real-Time Internal Battery Temperature Monitoring  (Relectrify)
Description:
Our organisation observes a rapid shift in the industry toward large-format prismatic
battery cells to increase energy density in Battery Energy Storage Systems BESS.
However, a critical safety bottleneck remains: these large cells develop severe internal
thermal gradients. During extreme fast charging XFC, the internal core can be
significantly hotter than the surface. 
This issue is further exacerbated by the choice of thermal management strategy. For
instance, while standard side-surface cooling is cost-effective, it often worsens radial
thermal gradients due to the cell's poor radial thermal conductivity. Conversely, tab
cooling (bottom cooling) addresses axial heat generation but requires precise control to
prevent localised hot spots. Current Battery Management Systems BMS rely on a limited
number of temperature sensors, leaving them "blind" to these complex multi-dimensional
gradients. Detecting these gradients is not just a safety requirement; it is a critical
feedback variable that informs better pack design (e.g., cooling sizing) and advanced
control strategies (e.g., gradient-sensitive fast charging), which can extend cell life. 
2. Project Goal 
The objective of this project is to design and validate a lightweight Thermal Gradient
Observer (a "Virtual Sensor") that runs on standard embedded microcontrollers. Instead
of merely estimating a single core temperature, the student will develop an algorithm that
estimates the spatial thermal gradients across the different dimensions (radial and axial)
of the battery cell in real-time, using only standard current and surface temperature
signals. 
3. Proposed Scope of Work 
The successful student(s) will be responsible for the following key phases:
● Phase 1 High-Fidelity Baseline Modeling - develop or utilize a high-fidelity 3D Finite
Element Analysis FEA thermal model (using tools like Matlab or Python) to simulate
the "ground truth" thermal behavior of a cell under different load profiles. This will
serve as the validation dataset.
● Phase 2 Reduced-Order Modeling - derive a computationally efficient Thermal
Equivalent Circuit Model. The student must simplify the complex 3D geometry into a

captures the dominant thermal dynamics while remaining mathematically simple. 
● Phase 3 Algorithm Implementation - design a closed-loop state observer (e.g.,
Kalman Filter or Luenberger Observer) in MATLAB/Simulink or Python. This algorithm
must fuse the simplified model with simulated sensor feedback to dynamically

● Phase 4 Validation & Benchmarking - verify the algorithm's performance against

4. Significance to Industry 
This project addresses a high-priority R&D topic. A successful outcome will demonstrate
how "Digital Twin" concepts can be deployed on low-cost hardware. The resulting
algorithms could inform next-generation BMS and thermal control architectures.

Project Title: Knowledge Graphs as Sovereign Data Infrastructure for Customary Land Tenure in the Pacific
Description:
Land information systems across the Pacific rely on relational database architectures that impose fixed schemas designed for statutory and freehold tenure. Customary tenure systems, which govern most land in Pacific Island countries, operate through overlapping use rights, clan and kinship-based entitlements, and oral or practice-based evidence. When forced into relational schemas, this complexity is not only simplified, it can become distorted in ways that undermine community tenure security and data sovereignty. As Pacific governments invest in land information modernisation, the choice of data model is a governance decision with lasting consequences for customary communities.

Students undertaking this project will need knowledge of database design and data modelling, graph database technologies, land administration concepts, and an understanding of Indigenous and customary data sovereignty principles including the CARE Principles. The investigation will require critical comparison of relational and graph-based approaches, and participatory or document-based inquiry into how customary tenure relationships are currently represented in a Solomon Islands or Fiji case study context.

The expected outcome is a prototype knowledge graph model for customary tenure that demonstrates how graph architectures can accommodate tenure complexity that relational schemas cannot, together with an assessment of the conditions under which such a model could interface with state systems while preserving community control over data and relational logic.

Project Title: Beyond Slope and Irradiance: Integrating Heterogeneous Tenure Data into Renewable Energy Site Suitability Models in India (or Nepal) (Landstack)
Description:
India’s plan to reach 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 relies on site selection processes that draw on spatial datasets built for revenue administration and forest governance, not energy infrastructure planning. These datasets are heterogeneous in provenance, coordinate reference systems, and classification schemes, and carry significant coverage gaps in areas governed by customary, tribal, and community tenure. When developers treat them as authoritative without integration or quality assessment, communities with legitimate but unregistered claims — particularly Adivasi and forest-dependent tribal groups — risk being rendered invisible through data infrastructure that was never designed to represent them. These datasets encode assumptions about which land uses and tenure types are legible, and those assumptions shape which communities bear the costs of energy transition. 

Students undertaking this project will need skills in spatial data integration and conflation, multi-criteria site suitability modelling, remote sensing and land cover classification, and sensitivity analysis. Understanding of Indian (or Nepalese) land tenure frameworks will be necessary context for interpreting integration challenges and coverage gaps.

The expected outcome is a replicable spatial data engineering framework for tenure-aware renewable energy site analysis, including documented integration methodology, sensitivity results showing how suitability scores shift under different tenure data assumptions, and a map of where data infrastructure gaps concentrate exposure to misclassification.

Project Title: Agentic AI versus authoritative data: a bounded spatial data quality assessment of exposure to error in OpenStreetMap using freight routing over a Victorian study area  (Department of Transport and Planning)
Description:
Critical freight infrastructure in Victoria increasingly depends on routing systems built on OpenStreetMap rather than authoritative Vicmap Transport data. OSM's community-based quality controls were designed for human adversaries whose behaviour is detectable and whose effort is scarce. Agentic AI breaks these assumptions: machine-scale actors can introduce or amplify errors at speed, vary behaviour to evade detection, and target precisely the low-traffic rural locations where correction is slowest, i.e., where the consequences of routing error in freight logistics are asymmetric. As AI-generated content enters OSM at scale, the gap between crowdsourced and authoritative data becomes a systemic infrastructure risk that has not yet been formally characterised.

Students undertaking this project will need skills in spatial data conflation, topological validation, accuracy assessment, and GIS analysis. Familiarity with OSM data structures and edit history APIs, and an understanding of risk assessment frameworks, will be essential. All work is conducted on a local OSM mirror and public data extracts; the live map is not touched.

The expected outcome is a replicable risk assessment methodology and a risk map of the study area showing where divergence between OSM and Vicmap Transport is greatest, where discrepancies persist longest, and where reliance on crowdsourced data carries the highest consequence for freight routing. The findings should be directly actionable by authoritative mapping agencies confronting this emerging data quality challenge.

Project Title: Improving Beach Safety Through Smart Coastal Monitoring
Description: Australia’s beaches are enjoyed by millions of people every year, but they also present significant hazards. Reducing coastal drowning is a national priority, yet it is impossible for lifesavers to continuously monitor the vast extent of Australia’s coastline. This project will investigate how shore-based cameras can be used to monitor nearshore conditions, including waves and rip currents. Using images captured in the visible spectrum from cameras installed at, for example, a surf lifesaving club, you will explore and validate techniques to estimate key environmental parameters that describe changing beach conditions. The knowledge gained will contribute to the development of next-generation coastal monitoring systems capable of providing timely information on hazardous conditions to support lifesavers and help beachgoers make safer decisions. The project offers hands-on experience in coastal engineering, computer vision, image analysis, and environmental monitoring, while contributing to research with the potential to make Australia’s beaches safer.

Project Title: Orbital spacecraft manoeuvring via stationary action and optimal control
Description: The Hohmann transfer is a classical orbital manoeuvre in spacecraft trajectory planning for transferring between different orbits of one or more gravitational bodies. A simple transfer between two distinct coplanar circular orbits around a single body yields an elliptical trajectory that is tangential to both orbits, with initiation and termination delineated by velocity changes imparted by impulsive engine burns. As the interim trajectory evolves exclusively due to the pervading gravitational field, it is energy conserving, and so can be described by the principle of stationary action. This description allows such transfers to be generalized to spacecraft navigating in more complex gravitational environments. In this project, the principle of stationary action will be embedded within an optimal control formulation of a design problem for minimal propellant orbital transfers. It will investigate and leverage existing and new tools for the solution of optimal control problems, and consider the feasibility and realisation of open-loop and closed-loop designs for such transfers.

Project Title: Electromagnetic Geophysical Methods for Subsurface Exploration
Description:
This project includes ground exploration with geophysical methods, and data interpretation, while you will develop soft skills like survey planning and collaborating with the industry. 

More specifically, the students are getting familiar with 3 electromagnetic geophysical exploration methods, namely Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR), EM Loupe, and Electrical Resistivity Tomography (ERT) measurements on campus and in real field conditions.
GPR: https://www.sensoft.ca/products/pulseekko- pro/overview-pulseekko /
EM Loupe:
https://www.loupegeophysics.com.au/index.php/mining- applications/
ERT: https://guidelinegeo.com/products/abem/abem-terrameter-ls-2/ 

First, you will be trained to collect data using these instruments by running some trial surveys at the university or in a nearby area. Then, you will get access to the data processing software. 

Once you are familiar with instrument operation and data processing, you will take part in some actual field surveys (2 or 3) in different environments (ex. mining site/ quarry/ agricultural land). These non-invasive field surveys may aim to identify geological layers, voids, and water tables by conducting scans from the ground surface and to position them in aerial maps. Some of this fieldwork will be delivered as collaborative projects with the industry, which will add more value to your CV.  

The group may get an opportunity to work with geophysics and geotechnical experts and ATC Williams and/or GHD. They will be thrilled to host you and potentially hire you as a graduate engineer if the job is performed at a high standard.

For further inquiries: hashan.korala@student.unimelb.edu.au

Project Title: TEMRover : Autonomous Ground Exploration Rover equipped with EM Loupe
Description:
Electromagnetic geophysical methods are non-invasive ground exploration techniques used across mining, agriculture, and hydrology. Advances in robotics, automation, and AI are opening new avenues for autonomous subsurface exploration.
In this project, you will join an ongoing effort to develop an autonomous ground exploration system combining the Scout 2.0 rover (AgileX Robotics) with EM Loupe electromagnetic sensing.
•	Scout 2.0: https://global.agilex.ai/products/scout-2-0
•	EM Loupe: https://www.loupegeophysics.com.au/index.php/mining-applications/

Mechanical Design and Fabrication
A conceptual design for the EM Loupe towing mechanism exists and is undergoing physical model testing. You will fabricate the towing cart(s), gaining hands-on experience in mechanical design and manufacturing.
Autonomous Navigation and Motion Control
The autonomous system is at an early stage of development. Your core technical contribution will be to:
•	Complete the autonomous navigation module, building on the current partial implementation
•	Design the motion control system governing rover-cart coordination, including path tracking and stability while towing the EM Loupe payload
Noise Characterization and Mitigation
A key research contribution of this project is understanding how rover-induced noise (e.g., motor/electrical interference, motion vibration) affects EM Loupe data quality. You will:
•	Quantify noise sources introduced by the rover platform during towed data acquisition, comparing against manual (non-motorized) survey baselines
•	Develop and apply data processing techniques to mitigate this noise, improving signal quality of the recovered EM data
Field Deployment
Following trial runs near the University to validate the integrated system, you will optimize performance and deploy for field survey(s) — likely two site visits — with objectives such as groundwater exploration or geological survey mapping via geophysical scans.
Data Processing and Analysis
You will process geophysical data using commercial industry software and, if scope allows, develop your own data-driven models to support subsurface interpretation.
Project Scope
Design, fabrication, autonomous system development, field deployment, and data interpretation — with noise quantification/mitigation forming the project's distinct technical and research contribution.

For further inquiries: hashan.korala@student.unimelb.edu.au

Project Title: Microfibre Emissions from Indoor Line Drying of Household Textiles
Description:
Background:
Microfibre emissions from textiles are an emerging environmental concern due to their release into air, water, and soil during everyday use and care. While previous research has focused on emissions from washing and tumble drying, indoor line drying—a widely used, energy-efficient alternative—remains largely unstudied. Drying clothes indoors may release airborne microfibres into enclosed environments, contributing to human inhalation exposure. This knowledge gap limits our understanding of the environmental and health implications of common laundry practices.

Project Scope:
This project will experimentally quantify and characterise airborne microfibre emissions generated during indoor line drying under representative household conditions. The study will develop a laboratory testing protocol and investigate the effects of washing method (machine vs. hand washing), textile type (synthetic, natural, semi-synthetic, and blended), and garment loading on microfibre emissions. Emissions will be quantified by number and mass, while fibre size, morphology, and material composition will be analysed using microscopy and advanced techniques, including Pyrolysis-GC-Orbitrap-MS.

Expected Outcomes:
The project will generate indicative emission factors for indoor line drying and improve understanding of how textile type and laundry practices influence airborne microfibre release. The findings will support more comprehensive life cycle and exposure assessments of household laundry practices and provide evidence to inform strategies for reducing indoor microfibre emissions.

Project Title: Decarbonising Australian Road Freight (National Transport Research Organisation)
Description:
This project will develop an Australia-specific, evidence-based framework to accelerate the decarbonisation of road freight by identifying where electrification is most feasible, cost-effective, and operationally practical across diverse freight segments. The research recognises that different vehicle types, routes, fleet structures, and operating conditions require tailored pathways rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. The project will be delivered through three key steps:
Freight Segmentation – define and classify Australian road freight operations using criteria such as route length, location, payload, fleet composition, operator structure, and company size;
Case Study Development – create representative freight operating archetypes and case studies that reflect the diversity of Australian freight tasks and support comparative assessment of low- and zero-emission technologies; and
Proof of Concept Model Development – Develop a tool to evaluate technical, operational, environmental, and economic factors, including vehicle performance, charging requirements, infrastructure needs, payload impacts, and regulatory considerations, to identify priority opportunities and inform industry investment and government policy.
 
The outcome will be a practical framework and supporting prototype tool that supports targeted deployment of electrified freight solutions and provides a scalable pathway to achieving Australia’s road freight decarbonisation goals.

Project Title: Cap System for Helical Pile Foundations in Transmission Infrastructure (Solidity)
Description:
Transmission infrastructure increasingly requires foundation systems that can be installed quickly, with reduced spoil, reduced disturbance and predictable connection details. Helical piles can provide an efficient foundation option for compression, tension and lateral actions, but the interface between the pile and the transmission structure is often project-specific. 

This project will investigate a modular precast concrete cap or steel fabricated cap that can connect one or more helical piles to transmission infrastructure, with a focus on practical constructability rather than final certified design. Students will review relevant foundation load paths, pile head tolerances, transport and lifting constraints, reinforcement detailing, grout pockets, anchor arrangements and the interface between steel pile shafts and concrete/steel components. The project should develop a bounded concept suitable for representative load cases nominated by Solidity, rather than trying to solve every transmission foundation condition. Students will compare several concept options and identify the advantages, limitations and testing requirements for each. 

The industry partner Solidity provides background on helical pile systems, typical pile geometries, installation tolerances, manufacturing considerations and non-confidential lessons from energy infrastructure projects. The desired outcome is a Phase 1 concept package that helps determine whether a precast modular cap or steel fabricated is technically promising and commercially practical enough for further engineering development, prototyping or full-scale testing.
