Project Title: Sensitivity of Modelled Shoreline Response to Sediment Grain-Size Variability in Port Phillip Bay
Description: The size of sediment grains, such as sand and seabed material, can affect how easily sediment moves and how the shoreline changes. Sediment grain size can affect shoreline response directly by controlling sediment mobility, and indirectly by modifying bed roughness, wave dissipation, currents, and nearshore water levels. However, coastal models often use a single representative grain-size value, which may overlook natural textural variations across coastal profiles. This project will investigate how realistic grain-size variations affect simulated shoreline response in Port Phillip Bay using XBeach, a coastal morphodynamic model. Representative grain-size scenarios will be developed from available sediment data, while wave and water-level forcing will be kept constant. By comparing erosion, accretion, and shoreline change under different grain-size settings, the project will assess the importance of site-specific sediment information for coastal modelling and shoreline management.

Project Title: Robotic Solar Deployment Across Australia's Renewable Energy Zones (Luminous Robotics)
Description:
This industry based Capstone project provides an opportunity to work with leading robotics company Luminous Robotics to work on solar energy installation. The students have flexibility to select the below 3 aspects or something close: 

Model and compare robotic solar module installation (LUMI Install) against manual installation and human-operated lifting equipment under Australian utility-scale conditions, accounting for local labour rates, site remoteness, climate and programme structures. The project would model installation rates, labour hours, equipment use, site logistics, programme duration, cost per module/MW, diesel displacement, emissions reduction and impact on levelised cost of energy (LCOE), capturing direct cost savings, schedule acceleration and module degradation effects.. 
Students would develop a suitability framework identifying which project characteristics (site size, tracker type, module format, terrain, location, programme constraints) favour each installation method, and use sensitivity analysis to identify which performance parameters offer the greatest opportunity for improvement.

Quantify the reduction in manual handling and ergonomic injury risk achievable through robotic solar module installation in the Australian WHS context. 
Students would develop a task-level breakdown of manual and LUMI-assisted installation methods, quantify differences in lifting frequency, load handling, repetition and postural and heat stress exposure using recognised ergonomic assessment tools, and estimate the corresponding injury risk reduction using Safe Work Australia claims data for construction manual handling. The project would also identify new risks introduced by human-robot interaction on site and assess the net safety case for robotic deployment.

Analyse how construction equipment and robotic installation fleets are mobilised to utility-scale solar projects in Australia, and design an optimal depot network to service the forward project pipeline. Using public pipeline data (AEMO, ARENA, Clean Energy Council) and declared Renewable Energy Zones, students would model transport and mobilisation costs, fleet utilisation, service radii and workforce availability to recommend depot locations and a deployment strategy as the robotic fleet scales.

Project Title: Towards a Robotic and AI-Enabled Autonomous Chemical Laboratory
Description:
Background
Robotics and Artificial intelligence have the potential to transform the future of chemical research. Here, autonomous chemical laboratories are emerging as a new paradigm that combines robotic systems, intelligent sensing, and AI-driven decision making to perform experiments with minimal human intervention. These laboratories have the potential to significantly accelerate chemical synthesis, materials discovery, and scientific innovation while improving safety, efficiency, and experimental repeatability.
This project forms part of an exciting research initiative to develop an autonomous chemical laboratory at the University of Melbourne. Previous capstone projects have developed a dexterous robotic hand for laboratory manipulation, while a mobile robotic platform equipped with a robotic manipulator is currently under development. The next challenge is to integrate these robotic systems into a unified autonomous laboratory platform.

Project Description
The objective of this project is to integrate a mobile unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), a robotic manipulator, and a dexterous robotic hand into a single intelligent robotic platform capable of autonomously performing laboratory tasks.
The integrated robotic system will navigate autonomously within the laboratory, transport test tubes between workstations, manipulate laboratory equipment, open and close test tube lids, and accurately place samples into chemical testing instruments. Students will develop the software architecture and control framework required to coordinate multiple robotic subsystems, enabling them to operate safely, reliably, and efficiently as a single autonomous laboratory assistant.
The project will involve robotic system integration, autonomous navigation, robot manipulation, motion planning, perception, and task scheduling. Students will gain hands-on experience with state-of-the-art robotic hardware and software while contributing to the development of a next-generation autonomous chemical laboratory.

Expected Outcomes
The successful project will demonstrate an integrated autonomous robotic system capable of performing laboratory sample handling and manipulation with minimal human intervention. The resulting platform will provide an important foundation for future AI-driven autonomous chemical synthesis, high-throughput experimentation, and accelerated materials discovery.
This project is ideal for students with interests in robotics, mechatronics, artificial intelligence, computer vision, autonomous systems, and intelligent automation. Students will have the opportunity to work on cutting-edge robotic technologies with direct applications in the future of scientific research.

Project Title: Systems-Focused Educational Design
Description:
Engineering knowledge is heterogeneous — even within a single discipline. Key concepts that are tightly interrelated are often taught in separate subjects, so students can struggle to see the connections needed to analyse, design and operate real systems.
The objective of this project is to bridge those gaps by developing a tangible engineering system (e.g., a robotic prosthetic arm) that can be decomposed into reusable subsystems for teaching across different subjects. By explicitly connecting these subsystems within a single real-world application, students develop an integrated understanding of engineering systems while acquiring the technical skills taught in each individual subject. The type of educational content will be co-developed with educators. 
The expected outcomes of the project are:
-	Idea generation 
-	Selecting or developing a real system
-	Identify learning objectives across multiple subjects
-	Design and implement one or more technical solutions 
-	Documentation for instructors
-	Educational task development and testing.
Skills you will develop
-	Systems integration and multidisciplinary design
-	CAD and rapid prototyping, materials and manufacturing choices
-	Sensors, actuators and embedded programming
-	Control design, signal processing and simulation 
-	Technical communication, curriculum design and assessment creation
-	Project management and teamwork

Project Title: Mixed Reality for Collaborative and Generative Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Shape Design
Description:
The early-stage design of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) morphology is a cognitively demanding task, requiring designers to navigate a high-dimensional design space and balance trade-offs among aerodynamic performance, structural integrity, weight, and stability. For remote, collaborative teams, this process is further strained by the spatial limitations of flat screen-sharing interfaces, which constrain how multiple stakeholders can engage with and manipulate 3D geometry. While mixed reality (MR) offers intuitive 3D visualisation and interaction, and generative design (GD) algorithms can rapidly produce many design options, their confluence and how that combined capability might influence designer behaviour, collaboration quality, and design outcomes in engineering design remains underexplored [1].
Recent systematic reviews have shown that MR remote collaboration holds great potential across industrial domains including design review and co-design [1], yet comprehensive empirical studies on MR-integrated generative design workflows are scarce. Similarly, while frameworks have been proposed for power dynamics in AR/MR-aided collaborative design and AI-augmented multimodal collaborative design, the specific intersection of MR spatial interaction, generative algorithms, and engineering design cognition has received limited attention.
The goal of this Capstone project is to establish a research testbed that integrates a parametric generative UAV model into a shared MR workspace, serving as a platform for experimentally probing how shared spatial interaction and generative feedback influence remote design collaboration, solution quality, and iterative efficiency.

Background 
Mixed Reality. MR technologies encompassing augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) are increasingly recognised for their ability to create shared immersive and interactive environments that decrease travel costs, save time, and facilitate more effective remote collaboration [1]. Research has demonstrated that MR can provide a more engaging end-user experience for product configuration, and tangible MR systems may facilitate problem-solving and improve design error detection. 
Generative Design. Generative design (GD) represents a paradigm shift in engineering, utilising AI algorithms to computationally explore the design space. This shift drastically changes the role of the human designer, adding GD to the traditional design process. However, concerns remain about AI’s potential to diminish designers’ critical thinking and reasoning skills. Recent work has emphasised the importance of human-centred generative design frameworks that support concept creation and evaluation while keeping designers in the loop [2]. The integration of MR with GD enables symbiotic interaction between virtual and real spaces, allowing real-time design modification, yet empirical studies on how such integration affects design cognition and collaboration quality are scarce.
UAV Design. UAV design is an ideal domain for this investigation due to its inherently multi-objective nature: designers must balance aerodynamic performance, structural integrity, weight, and stability often with competing requirements. Parametric modelling of UAV morphology allows systematic exploration of this design space, while lightweight performance calculators (e.g., lift and drag estimation) provide immediate quantitative feedback. This makes UAV design a rich context for studying how MR-mediated generative feedback influences design exploration and decision-making.

Academic Supervisor
Xingang Li, Lecturer, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Melbourne
Adelaide Genay, Lecturer, Computer Graphics & Visualisation, CIS, University of Melbourne
Bingran Wang, Lecturer, Aeronautical Engineering, University of Sydney
Yunlong Tang, Senior Lecturer, Materials Science and Engineering, Monash University

Methods
Part A: Literature Review and Interaction Framework (Months 1–2)
Conduct a systematic review of existing studies on collaborative design in shared 3D workspaces, with particular focus on: 1) Interaction patterns in remote MR collaboration (turn-taking, attention allocation, gesture use); 2) Power dynamics and stakeholder engagement in AR/MR-aided co-design; 3) Human-AI collaboration frameworks in generative design; 4) Usability evaluation protocols for MR collaborative systems.
Synthesise findings into a design requirements document that informs the prototype development. Identify key metrics for evaluating collaboration quality (e.g., task completion time, design iteration count, solution diversity, user satisfaction).

Part B: Core MR Collaboration Prototype (Months 3–6)
Build a working MR prototype using Unity and a head-mounted display (e.g., Meta Quest 3) where two remote users can: 1) Enter the same virtual room; 2) See each other as simple avatars (with head and hand tracking); 3) Simultaneously reach in and adjust the same UAV wing or body parameters; 4) View shared 3D model updates in real time
The prototype will incorporate: 1) Networked synchronisation of 3D object transformations; 2) Hand-tracking for intuitive manipulation (grab, scale, rotate); 3) Simple avatar representation with positional audio for spatial awareness; 4) Undo/redo functionality to support iterative exploration

Part C: Generative Function Integration (Months 7–10)
Integrate a parametric generative UAV model that can produce design variations based on user-specified objectives. Key features: 1) Parametric UAV geometry model (wing span, chord, sweep, fuselage dimensions, tail configuration); 2) Lightweight performance calculator providing real-time estimates of lift, drag, weight, and stability margins; 3) Dual interaction modalities: a) Direct 3D manipulation: Users grab and adjust geometric features of the UAV model; b) Performance graph interaction: Users drag points on 2D trade-off curves (e.g., speed vs. stability, lift vs. drag) and see the 3D form update in real time.
This dual-mode interaction is designed to address a known concern in generative design: that AI-generated solutions may reduce designers’ active cognitive engagement. By allowing designers to interact with both the shape and the performance trade-offs, the system keeps designers as active decision-makers rather than passive evaluators.

Part D: User Study and Evaluation (Months 11–12)
Design and conduct a controlled experiment comparing: 1) Condition A (Baseline): Remote collaboration using traditional screen-sharing (e.g., Zoom + CAD); 2) Condition B (MR only): Remote collaboration in MR without generative feedback; 3) Condition C (MR + Generative): Remote collaboration in MR with generative feedback and performance graph interaction. This can be implemented in a small scale to have a basic understanding of 1) Collaboration quality: Turn-taking frequency, verbal communication patterns, co-presence perception; 2) Design outcomes: Solution quality (performance metrics), design diversity, iteration count; 3) User experience: Cognitive load, satisfaction, perceived usefulness.

Part E: 3D Printing and Engineering Evaluation (Optimal)
Select optimal designs from the user study for 3D printing. Conduct basic structural and aerodynamic validation (e.g., wind tunnel testing) to ground-truth the performance calculator’s predictions.

Expected Outcomes:
1.  A functional research testbed for studying MR-mediated collaborative generative design
2.  Empirical evidence on how MR spatial interaction and generative feedback influence remote design collaboration, solution quality, and iterative efficiency
3.  Design guidelines for future MR + generative design systems in engineering contexts

References
[1]	Wang, P., Yang, H., Billinghurst, M., Zhao, S., Wang, Y., Liu, Z., and Zhang, Y., 2025, “A Survey on XR Remote Collaboration in Industry,” Journal of Manufacturing Systems, 81, pp. 49–74. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmsy.2025.05.016.
[2]	Demirel, H. O., Goldstein, M. H., Li, X., and Sha, Z., 2023, “Human-Centered Generative Design Framework: An Early Design Framework to Support Concept Creation and Evaluation,” International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction, pp. 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2023.2171489.



Expected Outcomes:
1.  A functional research testbed for studying MR-mediated collaborative generative design
2.  Empirical evidence on how MR spatial interaction and generative feedback influence remote design collaboration, solution quality, and iterative efficiency
3.  Design guidelines for future MR + generative design systems in engineering contexts

Project Title: AI-Powered Property Decision Support System for Intelligent Home Selection
Description:
a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Purchasing a home requires buyers to assess property features, neighbourhood conditions, planning controls, market trends and future investment potential. Existing property platforms mainly rely on predefined filters and require users to manually interpret listing images, advertisement descriptions, planning information and market data. This project will investigate how artificial intelligence can integrate and analyse these different sources of information to support more informed and personalised property selection.

b) Why is this issue important?
Home purchasing is a major financial decision, but buyers often lack the time, technical knowledge and access to integrated information needed to evaluate properties properly. Important factors such as renovation quality, planning restrictions, environmental risks, development potential, rental performance and neighbourhood accessibility may not be clearly presented in property listings. An intelligent decision support system could improve transparency, reduce information overload and help buyers compare properties using evidence that better reflects their needs and priorities.

c) The objectives of this research project is to develop a prototype to 1: Facilitate property search based on user requirements. 2: Calculate the current value of a property. 3:Consider growth and investment.

d) What are the key skills or knowledge needed to investigate the issue?
The project will require knowledge of artificial intelligence, Large Language Models, and machine learning. Skills in web application development, database design, API integration and data visualisation will also be useful. The project may involve analysing property images and advertisement descriptions, integrating zoning and planning information, examining neighbourhood characteristics, and comparing properties with recent sales and rental transactions. An understanding of model evaluation, data privacy, bias and responsible AI will also be important.

e) What is the expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a prototype online property decision support system that allows users to describe their preferred property using natural language. The system will interpret the user’s requirements, retrieve suitable properties and provide personalised recommendations supported by evidence from property listings, images, planning data, spatial information and market transactions. The prototype may provide insights into property condition, estimated market value, rental potential, planning opportunities, development constraints and neighbourhood suitability. The project will also evaluate the accuracy, usefulness and limitations of the proposed system.

Project Title: AI-Based Feature Extraction and Change Detection within Property Boundaries Using Aerial Imagery
Description:
AI-Based Feature Extraction and Change Detection within Property Boundaries Using Aerial Imagery

a) What is the key issue or problem to be investigated?
Aerial imagery contains detailed information about buildings and surrounding features, but manually extracting this information for individual properties is time-consuming and difficult to maintain. This project will investigate how artificial intelligence, computer vision and spatial analysis can be used to automatically identify and extract all visible features located within a defined property or site boundary.

The system may generate spatial layers and attributes for features such as:

Building footprints and roof areas
Solar panels and rooftop equipment
Trees, vegetation and landscaped areas
Swimming pools
Driveways, paths and paved surfaces
Sheds, garages and other structures
Changes to buildings and other visible features over time

All analysis and outputs will be restricted to the supplied property boundary. Features located outside the boundary will not be extracted or assessed.

b) Why is this issue important?
Accurate and current information about buildings and property features is valuable for local government, urban planning, property assessment, environmental monitoring, emergency management and infrastructure planning. However, existing spatial datasets may be incomplete or become outdated as buildings and properties change.

An automated method could reduce the time and cost required to create and update property-level spatial information. It could also support consistent analysis across large numbers of properties while ensuring that each result remains limited to the relevant property boundary.

c) What are the key skills or knowledge needed to investigate the issue?
The project will require skills in computer vision, deep learning, image processing, remote sensing and spatial data analysis. Programming experience, preferably in Python, will be needed to process aerial imagery, apply or train AI models, and create GIS-compatible outputs.

Useful knowledge may include:

Object detection and image segmentation
GIS and spatial data processing
Aerial image interpretation
Deep learning frameworks
Spatial databases and web mapping
Accuracy assessment and model evaluation

The project should also consider image resolution, shadows, vegetation cover, boundary accuracy and other factors that may affect feature detection.

d) What is the expected outcome of the research?
The expected outcome is a prototype system that receives aerial imagery and a defined property boundary, then automatically extracts visible building and site features within that boundary.

The system should produce GIS-ready spatial layers and relevant attributes for the detected features. It should also include a change-detection method that compares aerial imagery from different dates and identifies changes within the same boundary, such as:

New buildings or extensions
Building removal or demolition
Installation or removal of solar panels
Changes in trees and vegetation
Addition or removal of pools, sheds or paved areas

The project should evaluate the accuracy of the extracted features and change-detection results using reference data or manual validation.

Project Title: Nature Inspired Hydrodynamic Drag and Noise Reduction and Control
Description: It has been known that the collective drag and noise generated from a group of objects moving together is much lower than an object in isolation.  For example,   computational models have shown that the carangiform motion of a group of fish can reduce flow-generated drag and noise compared to isolated individuals (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-024-02568-z).     Hence, the primary objective of this project is to understand how the drag and noise are influenced by the various spatial arrangements and dynamical motion of the school of fish.  The research will perform simulations on high performance computers and utilise state of the art tools from Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) research.

Project Title: Modelling of Atmospheric Convection using Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NODEs) (CSIRO)
Description: Climate change and Global warming have serious consequences to our planet’s ecosystems, human health, and global economies. Understanding the exchange of carbon dioxide (CO₂) between the Earth's atmosphere, oceans, and biosphere  plays an important role in how we approach the improvement of mathematical/statistical models for climate change.  Informed decisions about sustainable future requires,   good physical models for atmospheric convection.  It is commonly accepted that many of the mathematical models are in the form of a system of ordinary partial differential equations.  However, in many instances, the exact form of these equations are often not known apriori and can be difficult to derive from first principles. In this project, we will explore the feasibility of discovering dynamics of atmospheric convection using Neural Ordinary Differential equations (NODEs).    The analysis  will be carried out using “real world” data from measurements obtained with colleagues from CSIRO Environment, Aspendale.

Project Title: AI for systematic literature reviews: tools to improve the identification and extraction of evidence from the published literature
Description:
Systematic Literature Review (SR) is a powerful tool that has revolutionized research and clinical practice in the medical sciences over the last 50 years. In SR, published studies are treated as data points, and analyses are conducted across a set of literature to create powerful tests of hypotheses. The outcomes of SRs have been used to direct medical practice and research directions. Despite repeated calls and attempts to make SR a standard practice in environmental science and management, the heavy resource requirements of these reviews has largely prevented uptake.

Two particular steps of SR consume huge amounts of time: 1) the screening of literature returned from keyword searches of databases, and 2) the extraction of evidence from those references deemed to be relevant to the questions being asked. Traditionally, these steps have been conducted by reviewers reading through vast numbers of study abstracts and then dissecting papers in detail to extract the evidence.

Recent years have seen the proliferation of AI tools to improve the efficiency of the SR process, but these have again been skewed towards medical applications.

Research in this project could be taken in any or all of several directions:
1)	Assessing how well existing large language models (e.g. Chat GPT) can identify relevant research from large volumes published literature. This could be done either by submitting a collection of abstracts obtained through keyword searches to an LLM, or by direct searching of the literature using the LLM.
2)	Assessing how well existing LLMs can extract evidence from published papers (evidence consists of data ‘atoms’ such as experimental design, replication, result, effect size). 
3)	Assessing how well bespoke AI tools for SR can apply to environmental science literature when they have been developed with medical literature in mind.

It is intended to use the Eco Evidence method for ‘rapid evidence assessment’ as the SR method to which we apply these findings. Eco Evidence was developed to try to reduce the workload associated with ‘full’ SRs but has still seen limited uptake because of the resource requirements of reviews. A successful outcome could be used to update the Eco Evidence method in a new publication.

Project Title: Public electric vehicle charging infrastructure: An activity-oriented spatial assessment
Description:
Electric vehicle (EV) charging decisions and behaviour are closely intertwined with users’ travel patterns. Users unable to charge their EVs at home often travel to destinations with charging facilities and engage in nearby activities to make productive use of their time while charging. On the other hand, users with home charging access use public charging for occasional top-ups (i.e., opportunistic charging where users plug their EVs in charging facilities already available at their destinations) and to mitigate range anxiety. These relationships between charging and activity-travel behaviour highlight the need for activity-oriented planning of public charging infrastructure, enabling users to charge their EVs while simultaneously participating in various activities.  

As governments and industry players expand charging infrastructure to support EV uptake targets, it is crucial to assess how effectively current infrastructure facilitates activity-oriented charging. This assessment is crucial for informing future distribution strategies and improving user experience. Existing literature assessing charging distribution predominantly focuses on spatial accessibility to public charging stations in isolation, often overlooking the charging-activity-travel behaviour links.  

This capstone project aims to evaluate the relationship between public charging infrastructure distribution and spatial accessibility to diverse activity opportunities (e.g., retail centres, parks, sporting facilities) across Victoria (VIC) and New South Wales (NSW), Australia. In doing so, it determines to what extent existing public charging stations in VIC and NSW enable activity accessibility. Additionally, the analysis can reveal which areas, particularly those where cars are typically parked for extended periods, could benefit from the installation of EV chargers to facilitate simultaneous activity engagement and charging. 

The project will employ GIS spatial analysis using a cumulative opportunities accessibility measure to evaluate the activity-orientedness of current public charging infrastructure distribution. Expected outputs will include a set of maps visualising the spatial relationship between charging infrastructure and activity points. This project will identify gaps in current charging network and provide evidence-based recommendations for more effective, user-centred EV infrastructure planning.

Project Title: Aerodynamic Characterisation of Dimpled Surface Technology Applied to High-Speed Train Nose Geometry (AeroTec Power Pty Ltd)
Description:
Background and Objective
AeroTec Power Pty Ltd holds patented aerodynamic technology called the Dimpled Coverage Technology (DCT), which has been wind-tunnel tested for tennis rackets to quantify drag and lift coefficients across varying wind speeds and angles of attack. AeroTec is now seeking to extend this technology into wind turbines and the front-end (nose) geometry of high-speed trains. The Company wishes to engage The University of Melbourne to evaluate the feasibility, performance, and commercial potential of applying DCT to high-speed rail, with a long-term view to establishing a discrete entity around the trains and wind turbine verticals in which the capstone student may take a key role in it, supported by Braddon Capital and partner investment networks.

Project Aim
To adapt the methodology of AeroTec’s prior racket-based wind tunnel study by applying it to scaled high-speed train nose models, comparing a baseline (smooth) geometry against one or more DCT-treated variants, and to quantify the resulting aerodynamic performance differences relevant to high-speed rail operation.

Main Activities
The Capstone team will undertake the following activities:
•	Literature Review. Survey of high-speed train aerodynamics, the prior AeroTec UQ racket study, and the underlying physics of dimpled-surface drag reduction.
•	Model Design and Fabrication. Design a scaled high-speed train nose model (scaling ratio to be set by Melbourne wind tunnel test-section dimensions and target Reynolds-number range), with at least one baseline and one DCT-treated variant. Models to be 3D-printed or machined in-house. Geometry, dimple pattern, and surface finish to be agreed with AeroTec.
•	Wind Tunnel Test. Replicate the methodology of the UQ racket study at The University of Melbourne wind tunnel. Measure force coefficients across a sweep of wind speeds V and yaw angles θ representative of operational high-speed rail conditions, including crosswind scenarios. Where feasible, supplement force-balance measurements with surface-pressure tappings, and flow visualisation when possible.
•	Reporting. A final capstone report and an industry-facing technical report for AeroTec.

Project Title: Relationship between electric vehicle (EV) charging dissonance and EV adoption stage
Description:
Unlike the familiar, quick process of refuelling internal combustion engine vehicles, charging electric vehicle (EVs) introduces new behaviours and frictions. EV charging varies by location (e.g., at home, at workplaces, in shopping destinations, and along highways) and by duration (slow to fast chargers), so users often need to plan trips more deliberately to accommodate charging into their routines. This planning burden is amplified by range anxiety (i.e., the fear of running out of battery power during trips) and public charging anxiety (i.e., concerns about charger availability, reliability, or compatibility), and is especially acute for households without home charging access. These practical and psychological frictions (need for deliberate planning, range anxiety, public charging anxiety, lack of home charging access) together capture charging dissonance. Charging dissonance occurs when users are unable (or expect to not be able) to charge their EVs where, when, and how they want to, creating a mismatch between desire and reality. Understanding charging dissonance can reveal nuanced psycho-attitudinal barriers that may deter potential EV adopters or create ongoing friction for current EV owners.  

This capstone project aims to investigate how charging dissonance relates to EV adoption stage, comparing current EV owners, prospective EV owners, and non-EV intenders. Using an existing online survey of about 1,000 driving adults in VIC, NSW, and QLD, it will (1) compare charging dissonance dimensions and general EV attitudes across EV adoption cohorts to determine which frictions and attitudes differ most strongly by adoption stage, and (2) test whether charging dissonance dimensions influence EV adoption intention among non-EV owners. 

This project will produce interpretable statistical model outputs and translate them into targeted policy and practice recommendations, such as guidance on charger provision and behavioural or informational strategies, so the EV switch and daily use become easier across different adoption cohorts. With governments and industry players currently rolling out charging infrastructure, these timely, evidence-based recommendations can help prioritise investments and complementary measures to reduce charging dissonance and accelerate EV uptake.

Project Title: Operational Modal Analysis of Structures Using Acceleration Data (Sterling)
Description:
This project will investigate the use of acceleration measurements and Operational Modal Analysis (OMA) to evaluate the dynamic characteristics and condition of civil infrastructure. Structures such as bridges and buildings are continuously exposed to operational and environmental loads, including traffic, wind and human activity. Their vibration responses can be measured using accelerometers and analysed to identify natural frequencies, damping ratios and mode shapes.

The project will be undertaken in collaboration with Sterling, providing an industry-oriented context and an opportunity to investigate practical structural monitoring and asset-management applications. Subject to data availability and project requirements, the student may work with acceleration data collected from laboratory structures, field-monitored infrastructure or representative case studies provided through the collaboration.

The student will process and analyse acceleration time-history data using signal-processing and modal-identification techniques. Methods may include Fast Fourier Transform, Power Spectral Density estimation, Frequency Domain Decomposition and, where appropriate, Stochastic Subspace Identification. The project will also investigate the effects of sensor location, measurement duration, signal noise and operational or environmental variability on the reliability of the identified modal parameters.

The identified modal characteristics will be interpreted to evaluate structural behaviour and establish baseline dynamic performance. Where suitable datasets are available, the student may compare modal parameters across different monitoring periods or structural conditions to examine whether changes in frequency, damping or mode shape could indicate changes in stiffness, boundary conditions or structural condition.

Project Title: Emotional Intelligence in Engineering Education
Description:
Engineering education has traditionally emphasised technical knowledge, analytical thinking, and problem-solving skills. While these competencies remain essential, the contemporary engineering workplace increasingly requires graduates to demonstrate strong interpersonal abilities, leadership capabilities, and emotional intelligence (EI). Engineers are now expected to work effectively in multidisciplinary teams, communicate with diverse stakeholders, manage workplace relationships, and lead projects in complex and dynamic environments.

To ensure that university programs remain aligned with industry needs and prepare graduates for successful professional practice, ongoing curriculum review and enhancement are essential. Understanding the expectations of practising engineers and engineering employers is critical for identifying the attributes and skills that future graduates require. Despite strong technical preparation, many graduate engineers in Australia experience challenges when transitioning from university to the workforce, particularly in areas related to communication, teamwork, leadership, self-awareness, and relationship management. Identifying the factors contributing to this transition gap is vital for developing more industry-relevant engineering education programs.

This project aims to investigate industry expectations regarding emotional intelligence and its role in engineering practice, and to explore how EI can be more effectively integrated into engineering curricula. The study will examine the emotional intelligence competencies most valued by engineering professionals and employers, as well as the extent to which current engineering programs develop these capabilities. To gain rich industry insights, semi-structured interviews will be conducted with practising engineers, engineering managers, and industry leaders across diverse engineering sectors. These interviews will explore industry perceptions of EI, the challenges faced by graduate engineers, and recommendations for enhancing EI development within engineering education.

Project Title: AI Training Repository for Smart Meter Data Applications
Description: This Capstone project focuses on developing an open, well-structured training repository that demonstrates how artificial intelligence methods can be applied to smart meter data in power distribution networks. Using GitHub and Jupyter Notebooks, students will create clear, reproducible examples that demonstrate techniques such as neural networks and advanced linear regression. The repository will illustrate practical applications, including voltage estimation, what-if scenario analysis, and hosting capacity assessment using smart meter measurements. Emphasis will be placed on sound data-handling practices, transparent modelling assumptions, and clear documentation so that the material can be reused by students, researchers, and practitioners worldwide. The project aims to produce a technically sound educational resource that connects AI methods with real power system problems, supporting learning and experimentation in modern distribution network analysis.

Project Title: Foundation Models for Electrical Model-Free Voltage Calculations (Future Grid)
Description: Distribution companies require accurate voltage calculations to assess the effects of technologies such as rooftop solar, electric vehicles, and batteries. However, detailed electrical models of low-voltage networks are not always complete or sufficiently accurate. This Capstone project will investigate a foundation-model-inspired approach for estimating customer voltages using only realistic synthetic smart meter data (active power, reactive power, and voltage magnitude), without requiring electrical network models. Students will develop and train a common neural network using synthetic data from multiple low-voltage networks and assess whether the resulting model can be efficiently adapted to a previously unseen network using only a limited amount of additional data. Its performance will be compared with neural networks trained separately for each network, considering voltage-estimation accuracy, training-data requirements, and computational effort. The project will provide practical insights into whether reusable pretrained models could support scalable electrical model-free voltage calculations across distribution networks.

Project Title: Control of a permanent magnet synchronous machine
Description: The aim of the project is to develop the drive electronics for a three-phase permanent magnet synchronous motor.  Execution of the project will involve the design, simulation, and implementation of a DC source, an inverter, and embedded control system for the AC machine. The project provides scope to explore speed adaptation for the efficient operation of mechanical loads, and regenerative braking, for example.

Project Title: Environmental fluid dynamics: Simulating flow over rough topography using a super computer
Description:
Fluid flow over rough topography is widespread in environmental and industrial settings. Environmental applications include ocean currents over the seafloor or beneath ice, the atmospheric boundary layer over land, and water rushing over a riverbed. Numerically modelling rough topography is often difficult due to the complicated boundary condition. However, it is imperative to efficiently model these problems in a range of contexts. This project will simulate flow over rough topography using a computational fluid dynamics approach. The students will become familiar with the solver, run parallelised simulations, learn flow visualisation techniques and fluid physics involved with this complex flow. This project may include the opportunity to run simulations on Australia’s fastest supercomputer (NCI’s Gadi).

The first step of the project will be learning the solver and validation against standard fluid dynamics cases (such as turbulent channel flow). Then we will run a series of direct numerical simulations of a buoyancy-driven current with rough topography. The students will learn how to analyse the output data and use flow visualisation techniques. The simulations will test a variety of flow strengths (Reynolds numbers) while the rough topography can be varied by type (random roughness, grooves, scallops), size and amplitude. Expected deliverables are the validation of the solver, a series of simulations testing a parameter range (to be decided in collaboration with the students), visualisation and analysis of the flow, and (where possible) comparison against fluid theory. 

Note: if a strong student is particularly interested in this or similar environmental flow problems, there is a possibility of continuing this work into a PhD.

Project Title: Grounded Futures: Indigenous Innovation in the Afterlife of Aircrafts
Description:
Working in partnership with the Centre for Appropriate Technology (CfAT) and the Arrernte community, this project aims to identify and implement culturally and technologically appropriate ways to repurpose decommissioned aircraft components stored at the Alice Springs boneyard. Aircraft parts, as engineered objects, are designed for precision, strength, and endurance, yet their afterlife is often limited to recycling or narrow forms of reuse. This project explores a more expansive approach, framing material repurposing through Indigenous knowledge systems, values, and local needs.

A previous capstone team worked with CfAT on a design tool for culturally grounded ideation and began the process of generating and testing concepts for repurposing airline seats. Students in this capstone will build on this work by further developing, testing, and prototyping these concepts in partnership with CfAT to determine what appropriate applications for these components can be on Country.

Project Title: Surviving the Lunar Night: Enabling Rechargeable Energy Storage for the Moon (MP Space)
Description:
This project offers the opportunity to tackle one of the most challenging and topical problems in modern space engineering: keeping a lunar lander or rover operational throughout the two-week lunar night using rechargeable batteries, stored solar energy and innovative thermal-mechanical design.

Students will explore and compare advanced battery-cell technologies, develop battery-management strategies for extreme cold, and design integrated thermal and mechanical concepts that minimise heat loss while withstanding launch and landing loads. Particular attention will be given to mechanically supporting the battery while limiting conductive heat paths and using a small, controlled amount of internal heat dissipation to maintain safe temperatures throughout the 336-hour lunar night and subsequent daylight operations.

With support from an Australian battery-industry partner and the Melbourne Space Lab, students will work with representative cells and hardware to design and conduct characterisation tests addressing key design uncertainties, including insulation performance, conductive heat losses and low-temperature battery behaviour.

The project will develop practical skills in systems engineering, power and thermal subsystem design, mechanical design, experimental testing, verification and industry collaboration. Its outcomes may directly inform future small lunar landers and surface systems, while also contributing to advanced energy-storage and thermal-management technologies for other extreme environments.

Project Title: Autonomous Low-Cost Robotic System for Building Damage Detection, Floor Coverage, and Automated Reporting
Description:
This project will advance an existing Low-Cost (sub-AUD1000) Raspberry Pi 5–based robotic platform (LiDAR + depth camera) for fully autonomous building damage inspection in hazardous or non-accessible environments (such as post earthquake scenario). Previous work has already integrated ROS2 SLAM, YOLOv8m, and TF transforms to produce a georeferenced damage map over the SLAM-generated floor plan, but operates with limited damage data and without autonomous navigation or higher-level mission intelligence.

The proposed research focuses on three main objectives:

1. Enhanced damage detection on embedded hardware
    Expand and refine the building damage dataset (more materials, lighting, and damage types), then train and benchmark multiple YOLO variants (e.g. YOLOv8–YOLOv13) on the Raspberry Pi 5. Compare detection accuracy, real-time performance, and resource usage to identify the most effective configuration for on-board structural damage inspection.

2. Autonomous floor coverage and robust inspection runs
    Integrate ROS2 SLAM with the Nav2 stack and a coverage/exploration strategy to achieve unattended floor coverage in multi-room environments. The robot should plan and execute inspection missions without teleoperation, reliably revisiting and inspecting areas of interest. The existing damage mapping pipeline will be updated and validated under these autonomous runs.

3. Lightweight agentic reasoning for mission control and automated reporting
    Incorporate a compact reasoning model (e.g. Gemma or an API-based equivalent) for mission-level autonomy and human-facing outputs:
        a. Decide when an inspection mission is complete based on exploration coverage and detection confidence.
        b. Generate an automated inspection report summarising damage locations, types, and estimated severity, and providing an overall condition assessment suitable for civil engineering decision-makers.

The project will deliver and experimentally evaluate a low-cost, end-to-end autonomous inspection workflow, contributing to research in embedded deep learning for structural health monitoring, autonomous coverage-based inspection, and the added value of lightweight agentic reasoning for mission autonomy and reporting in built environments.

Project Title: Biomimetic vision using 3D printed waveguides
Description: Using optical ray-tracing and 3D printing, an optical system will be designed to allow light detection within a large solid angle, much like insects with compound eyes which can see "behind" them. By increasing the angle of view of simple cameras, different applications can be realised such as security, motion sensing, and autonomous vehicles.

Project Title: Acoustic trapping of microparticles
Description: A system shall be designed which allows the trapping and release of airborne microparticles, to be integrated with a microscope. This would allow automated sample handling of environmental microparticles and allow their monitoring via microscopy and spectroscopy.

Project Title: Trust, Redundancy, and Failure: A Testbed for Fault-Tolerant Time Synchronization in Networked Infrastructure
Description: Motivated by the July 2026 nationwide Telstra outage, in which a fault in the timing hierarchy of its network data centres was reported to have caused servers to revert to a clock nearly two decades in the past and cascade into failures across telecommunications, transport, and payment systems, this project builds a (simulation-based or physical) testbed for studying fault-tolerant time synchronization. The core synchronization logic draws on the classical fault-tolerant clock estimation framework of Marzullo and Owicki (1983), whose interval-intersection algorithm for combining multiple noisy time sources under bounded faults underlies the selection and clustering algorithm still used in NTPv4 today, and on Lamport and Melliar-Smith (1985), who established the theoretical bounds on how much source redundancy is required to tolerate faulty or Byzantine clocks in a distributed system. To model realistic failure modes rather than hypothetical ones, the project draws on Malhotra, Cohen, Brakke and Goldberg (2016), who demonstrate concrete on-path and off-path attacks capable of shifting client time via spoofed sources, low-rate denial-of-service, and IPv4 packet fragmentation, and on Bishop (1990), whose early security analysis of the NTP hierarchy illustrates how a single compromised synchronization path can isolate or mislead an entire downstream cohort of servers.

Project Title: Sensitivity of multiagent task allocation algorithms
Description: This research will consider the sensitivity of task allocation algorithms to uncertainty in the information available when the allocation decision is being made. The aim is to develop suboptimal algorithms that are less likely to change allocations when new information comes to light. Results will be demonstrated on industry relevant simulations.

Project Title: Wireless Environmental Sensing: A Solar-Powered LoRa Network
Description:
Ever wondered how a vineyard tracks soil moisture across hundreds of hectares, or how a city maps air quality street by street? This project puts you at the heart of that technology. You'll design and build a network of wireless sensor nodes that run unattended for weeks on solar power, beaming environmental data over kilometres using LoRa, the low-power radio standard behind real-world “internet of things” deployments.

The main component that will form part of this project is the node hardware: a solar-and-battery power system frugal enough to survive a Melbourne winter(!), laid out on a custom PCB. In parallel with the node design, you will need to design the communication protocol and run field testing that measures real range, signal strength, and reliability as you push the nodes further apart.

The nodes report to a gateway and cloud backend - turning the raw radio packets into live dashboards and automatic alerts that fire when readings cross a threshold. By the end of the project, you'll have a multi-node network deployed outdoors, running on sunlight, streaming live data to a screen.

Project Title: Enabling Circular Infrastructure through Repurposing Complex Product Systems: Mapping Knowledge Flows, Capabilities and Business Models
Description:
a) Key issue or problem to be investigated
The transition towards a circular economy requires new approaches for designing, managing and repurposing complex engineered products and infrastructure assets beyond their original lifecycle. While many industries possess valuable components, modules and materials that could potentially be reused or repurposed, significant barriers remain in translating technical possibilities into viable circular solutions.

This project investigates how knowledge, data and expertise need to flow between organisations to enable the repurposing of complex product systems (e.g., aerospace, energy, manufacturing and infrastructure components). It will explore the project management, design, certification and business model capabilities required to transform repurposing opportunities into commercially and strategically viable propositions.

b) Why this issue is important
Current linear approaches to infrastructure and industrial production contribute to resource depletion, waste generation and missed opportunities for retaining embedded value within existing assets. Circular economy approaches have the potential to reduce environmental impacts while creating new business opportunities through reuse, remanufacturing and cross-industry innovation.

However, successful circularity requires more than technical solutions. Organisations must coordinate across supply chains and industries, overcome certification and regulatory barriers, develop new value propositions, and establish new collaboration models. Understanding these enabling mechanisms is critical for accelerating circular innovation in engineering and infrastructure sectors.

c) Expected outcome of the research

The project is expected to develop:
A framework identifying the key capabilities and knowledge flows required for circular repurposing of complex engineering systems
Mapping of stakeholder ecosystems and potential collaboration pathways across industries
Identification of barriers and enablers for implementing circular business models
Case-based value propositions or pilot concepts demonstrating how repurposing opportunities could be translated into practice
Recommendations for future industry partnerships and larger-scale research opportunities

Project Title: AI-Powered Analysis of Biological Data
Description:
Google DeepMind's AlphaFold - the AI model awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry - solved one of biology's hardest computational problems: predicting the 3D structure of proteins with atomic precision. Its latest generation can now model how proteins interact within complexes, opening powerful new possibilities in medicine.
 
In this project, you will apply AlphaFold and related AI tools to study how antibodies from immune cells bind to viral proteins — such as those from SARS-CoV-2 or hepatitis C virus. By predicting and analysing these structures, you will identify and explore interaction patterns relevant to vaccine design and antibody-based therapeutics.
 
No biology background is required. The work is fundamentally about data, AI and machine learning models, and computation, and about applying rigorous engineering thinking to high-impact biomedical problems.
 
What you will learn
- Understanding of state of the art AI models such as AlphaFold
- How to prepare and run large computational jobs on advanced computing systems
- Practical skills in Python and data handling for health and biomedical data
- How to visualise and inspect 3D protein structures using standard tools

Project Title: Mapping, Localisation and Navigation  for an Autonomous Ground Robot Using Vision and LIDAR
Description:
Though highly informative, vision- and LIDAR-based sensors can significantly slow down the speed with which robots explore an area or navigate to a target. This is because the huge amount of data contained in each image must be transmitted to a distant controller, or processed periodically by a small and limited on-board computer, before the next motion command can be issued.  In this project, you will investigate how to get a wheeled autonomous robot to efficiently map its surroundings, localise itself and search for a target of specified form and colour, using compressed visual and/or LIDAR measurements  and no AI. 

This will be done on a Clearpath Jackal four-wheeled robot:
https://clearpathrobotics.com/jackal-small-unmanned-ground-vehicle/ 
https://docs.clearpathrobotics.com/docs_robots/legacy/ros1_robots/outdoor_robots/jackal/tutorials_jackal/ 

Induction into the relevant laboratories will be required.

Suggested Reading:

Project Title: State Estimation for  Stochastic Systems with Infinite-Dimensional Measurements
Description:
This project investigates state estimation in discrete-time stochastic systems with finite-dimensional states and infinite-dimensional measurements. This is motivated by applications such as vision-based localisation and tracking for autonomous drones without GPS. The aim is to develop and implement Kalman filtering-like algorithms for real-time state estimation in such systems, with the measurement noise modeled as an infinite-dimensional random field. For systems with nonlinearities such as drones, extended Kalman-filtering algorithms will be developed and tested on real-world data sets. Methods of complexity reduction will be explored to enable real-time implementation at moderate to fast frame rates. 

This project suits students hoping to do a PhD.

Project Title: Forecasting of electricity prices for economic model predictive control of pumping in water supply systems.
Description: Energy costs associated with pumping in water distribution systems can be large. For that reason some water  companies buy their electricity  from the market without going through a retailer, and hence the electricity price is  randomly varying. In water distribution networks there are water storages which provides robustness in case of failures in pumps or pipelines, but they also allows operators to shift pumping from high price periods to low price periods. A promising strategy for reducing energy cost is to use economic model predictive control which requires forecast of the electricity prices. AEMO (Australian Energy Market Operator) provide publicly available forecasts. In this project you will model the forecast error using parameterised models such as AR and ARMA models, estimate the parameters in these models taking into account that they will be used in an economic model predictive control setting, and finally implement an economic model predictive control strategy for pumping operation.

Project Title: Bayesian data driven modelling and control
Description: In Bayesian data driven modelling, models of a dynamical system is estimated from data. Moreover, the unknown model parameters are assumed realisations of random variables and are assigned  prior distributions. In the end one obtain not only a nominal model of the system but also a posterior distribution of the unknown system parameters which quantifies the uncertainty in the model. This is useful when the model is going to be used for control and gives information about how much robustness (e.g. gain and phase margin) needs to be built into the controller. In this project you will explore Bayesian data driven modelling, and design controllers which takes the uncertainty in the model into account. Moreover, you will also explore how the data obtained when the system is operated in closed  loop with the designed controller can be used to improve the model and reduce the uncertainty. A new an improved controller can then be designed and implemented using the updated model.
